report:
**Conclusion: yes—if “heavy (ex-)smokers” means people at high risk who match screening criteria.** Randomized trials show that repeated *low-dose* CT (LDCT), rather than ordinary diagnostic CT, reduces deaths from lung cancer by finding more cancers while curable.

The U.S. NLST randomly assigned high-risk current/former smokers (55–74 years, at least 30 pack-years, and former smokers had quit within 15 years) to three annual LDCTs or chest X-rays. Lung-cancer mortality was 247 versus 309 deaths per 100,000 person-years: a **20.0% relative reduction** (95% CI 6.8–26.7%). This is strong causal evidence because the comparison was randomized—not simply a comparison of people who chose screening with those who did not.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21714641/

A second large randomized trial, NELSON, compared repeated volume-based LDCT with no screening in high-risk current and former smokers. At 10 years, lung-cancer mortality was **24% lower in men**; the estimate in women was a 33% reduction, but less precise because far fewer women participated. Its agreement with NLST materially strengthens the conclusion.  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1911793

This does **not** mean every former smoker benefits equally, nor that screening substitutes for quitting. The benefit/harm balance is favorable chiefly for people at sufficiently high risk and healthy enough for diagnostic work-up and potentially curative treatment. In the U.S., USPSTF recommends annual LDCT for adults **50–80** with **≥20 pack-years** who currently smoke or quit within 15 years, stopping when quitting exceeds 15 years or health limits curative treatment.  
https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/recommendation/lung-cancer-screening

Harms matter: false-positive findings, follow-up scans/procedures, radiation, incidental findings, anxiety, and overdiagnosis (Cochrane estimates CT-screening overdiagnosis at 18%). Screening should therefore occur in a structured program with shared decision-making.  
https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD013829_impact-computed-tomography-ct-lung-cancer-screening
